fields.title: Surma: Turning an Internal Tool into a Product
fields.summary: Management wants to sell Dispetcher to other carriers. Decide where to start.
fields.decisionPrompt: Where will you start, and what will you show the board in six months?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager of Dispetcher.
fields.brief/company: Surma is a fictional transport company: 60 trucks, long-haul. Dispetcher is its internal route planning tool, in use for three years.
fields.brief/context: The board of directors suggests selling Dispetcher to other carriers: 'the tool is ready, the market is big'. They allocate six months and three people. They also demand to 'add AI, everyone has it now'.
fields.brief/objective: Decide where to start turning the tool into a product.
fields.brief/constraints: Six months, three people, no separate sales budget.
fields.brief/task: Choose the first step and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Test first what kills the idea
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Every new concept has an assumption upon whose failure nothing else matters. Teams almost always start not with that, but with what they know how to do. The order of validation is the key decision at the start, and it is the cheapest: a conversation that takes six weeks saves four months of wasted development.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Three years in operation, eight Surma dispatchers use it daily.

Route planning, backhaul suggestions, driver and category tracking.

Surma's empty mileage decreased from 18% to 13.4% over two years.

Built around Surma's specifics: own routes, own fleet structure, integration with Surma's accounting.

No multi-tenancy: the system is designed for a single company, data is not separated.

Developers' estimate: data separation between companies — 3 months, decoupling from Surma's accounting — 1 month.

Three years of data accumulated on which backhauls actually get loaded on European routes.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Carriers with 30–80 trucks: about 4,000 of them, according to the industry association.

How they plan now: spreadsheets — the majority; notebooks — a noticeable part; expensive systems for large fleets — very few, they consider them overkill.

In five conversations with familiar carriers (directors, not dispatchers):
— 'empty mileage — yes, that hurts';
— 'but you carry cargo yourselves? so I'll be showing you my routes and clients?' — four out of five asked this;
— 'how much does it cost' — asked by two, both before the data question.

Two competitors in the market: one expensive for large fleets, the other is truck tracking without planning.

Industry association is ready to provide a platform for a pilot if the product is independent of the carrier.
fields.evidenceCards/2/title: What is behind the AI requirement
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
The board's wording: 'add AI, everyone has it now'.

In conversation, it turned out what they meant: the chairman read an article about demand forecasting in logistics.

What is actually possible with our data: predicting backhaul loads. Data — three years for 60 trucks, fewer than 40 observations for most routes.

Analyst's estimate: the prediction will work on Surma's routes, but not on new routes of other carriers until data accumulates.

What else is close by: invoice OCR during intake. Surma's dispatcher spends 6 minutes on manual entry per route, technology limitations are known, cost is calculated — 3 weeks of work.

Carriers never mentioned AI in conversations.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Surma's COO is against it: 'we will give our way of working to competitors'.

CFO believes the product will pay off in a year, but brought no calculations.

Lawyer raised a question: if we store other carriers' routes and carry cargo ourselves, do we need a separate legal entity? No answer yet.

Development wants to start with data separation — 'we will need it anyway'.

There is no sales function in the company: we sold shipping services, not software.

Deadline set by the board: show first paying clients in six months.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Test first what kills the idea
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: The issue of trust in a competitor carrier is more important than any development: test it with real carriers and on the legal setup, and start development only after.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
You state the most dangerous assumption out loud: a competitor carrier will give route data to a company that carries cargo itself. Four out of five have already asked this question themselves.
Over six weeks, you conduct twelve conversations and get an answer: nine are ready if the product is legally separated from Surma, data is not visible to the carrier, and this is confirmed by a contract. Three are not ready under any circumstances.
In parallel, the lawyer outlines a separate legal entity; the association confirms its readiness to provide a platform under this exact condition.
Only after this does development start data separation — three months — and you come to the board not with a promise, but with four prepayments from pilot carriers.
Regarding AI, you reframe the question into a product format: prediction on other routes won't work with fewer than 40 observations, but invoice OCR saves 6 minutes per route in three weeks. The board agrees.
Compromise: the first month and a half looked like talking without a single line of code, and the COO considered it a waste of time.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Development is right: multi-tenancy will be needed anyway. Three months for that, then decoupling from accounting, then sales.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Four months are spent on technical preparation, and it is done well.
When it comes to sales, what lay on the surface emerges: carriers do not want to give routes to a company that carries cargo itself. Four out of five asked about this before the work started.
A separate legal entity and an NDA take another two to three months, which do not fit into the six-month limit.
The board is shown a working system with no clients.
Compromise: what was definitely needed was built before checking if it was needed at all; the sequence cost the project.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The board asks for AI, and we have three years of backhaul load data. This will be our differentiator.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Four months of work yield a prediction that works well on Surma's routes and barely works on others: fewer than forty observations for most routes.
You can only show it to carriers using your own data, which amplifies the exact question to be feared: 'so you know where and what we carry?'.
Meanwhile, simple invoice OCR, which saves 6 minutes per route in three weeks, is not built.
Carriers never asked about AI.
Compromise: management's request was executed literally instead of being translated into a product question, and the chosen technology amplified the project's main risk.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Build a concept and launch a pilot with acquaintances
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Fill out a Lean Canvas, find two familiar carriers, and give them the tool as is, with manual data separation.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The canvas is put together in a day and brings value: it becomes clear that the unfair advantage is not a 'strong team', but three years of data on actually loaded backhauls.
The pilot with two familiar carriers starts in a month, without development, using manual separation.
One carrier works and is happy; the second leaves after three weeks — their CFO banned sharing routes with Surma. This is the exact risk, but you learn about it on a sample of two.
By six months, there is only one pilot client, nothing to generalize, and the legal setup is still not outlined.
Compromise: the right move — cheap validation instead of development — was made on a sample that was too small and too friendly.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: The concept does not highlight the assumption upon whose failure everything collapses
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Technology is evaluated on its own, not by the limitation it removes
